An ordinary sampling operation does not expose a deterministic differentiable path from its random output to distribution parameters. The gradient of an expectation also includes how the distribution changes; differentiating a fixed sampled value as a constant misses that dependence. For a Gaussian, sample parameter-independent $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and set $z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon$. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)

Now gradients pass through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ while averaging over fixed-noise draws: $\nabla_\phi\mathbb E_\epsilon f(z_\phi)=\mathbb E_\epsilon\nabla_\phi f(z_\phi)$ under suitable regularity. This is a pathwise estimator, often lower variance than a score-function estimator. It does not mean stochastic computation is inherently undifferentiable; it means the estimator must account for distributional dependence. Discrete sampling generally needs other estimators or relaxations, with their own bias/variance tradeoffs.
